Falling 1.03% to 7,341, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) marked its fourth day of consecutive losses, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) dropped 0.74% to 24,328 on technology sector weakness, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) tumbled 1.64% to 50,759.

Gold price dipped 0.18% to $3,849.20 as of U.S. market close, while the 10-Year Treasury yield edged down 3 basis points to 5.11% during a session in which energy stocks were the only real gainers, with financial services and healthcare stocks under the most pressure.

Today's biggest moves

Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) plummeted 9.45% as security jitters and further AI replacement fears combined to punish software stocks. UnitedHealth Group (NYSE:UNH) dropped 5.42% on sweeping anti-fraud proposals for Medicare & Medicaid. Crypto stocks, including Coinbase Global (NASDAQ:COIN) and Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD), tumbled as Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) continued its losing streak -- the leading crypto is now down over 20% in the past month.

What this means for investors

The recent string of technology outages that have hit air travel, banks, and other firms weighed further on stocks today, compounding (artificial intelligence) AI chip concerns and broader negative sentiment. Consumers are stockpiling essentials, which helped Costco Wholesale Corp (NASDAQ:COST)as Mizuho Securities just upped its price target on the stock.

Post-close earnings from Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) beat analyst expectations, offering some reassurance on AI infrastructure demand and boosting peers in after-hours trading. Investors are still digesting the impact of new U.S. measures restricting international access to advanced AI chips, not only for Nvidia but for the whole sector.

Stocks fell sharply again Tuesday, with tech shares dragging on the main indexes after a CNN report said the National Security Agency's (NSA) highly classified internal network was down. Wall Street was already skittish on technology after a slew of recent glitches, including the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounding all national flights last Friday and service outages at several big banks on Monday.

At the close, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.6% at 50,759, the broader S&P 500 was off 1.0% at 7,340, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was 0.7% lower at 24,328.

Salesforce (CRM) was the worst Dow Jones stock today, sinking 9.5% — its biggest one-day drop since May 30, 2024 — on broad-market headwinds. The cloud platform's slump also comes ahead of Anthropic's (ANT) market debut, with the large language model (LLM) provider set to begin trading on Thursday.

Read more: Anthropic IPO: Should You Buy ANT Stock?

Software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers took a big hit earlier this year on worries that AI will disrupt their business models, but many stabilized after Wall Street deemed these concerns overblown.

CRM, for one, is up nearly 30% since late June — and Stifel analyst J. Parker Lane thinks it has more room to run. Lane has a Buy rating and a $300 price target on Salesforce, representing implied upside of 54% to current levels.

Salesforce is feeling the SaaS heat ahead of Anthropic's final IPO pricing on Wednesday, prompting investors to question whether CEO Marc Benioff's company needs to exist at all.

CRM is down 9.5% at the time of writing.

HubSpot also fell 5%, while Workday dropped 4.5%, as investors worry that Claude is coming for all three companies' lunches. The sell-off likely reflects funds making room for the week's biggest mover, since Salesforce's latest results weren't all that bad.

The company beat estimates with $11.35 billion in revenue and $5.90 in non-GAAP EPS, and it continues to integrate AI into its products. The 80% EPS beat was largely due to Salesforce's strategic holdings in Anthropic, the same company behind today's sell-off. Salesforce reported that its Anthropic stake accounted for roughly 45% of its $11.3 billion strategic investment portfolio. A rough calculation suggests it holds approximately 86.3 million to 86.4 million in Anthropic shares. Salesforce will presumably hold the shares long term rather than sell them.

With $1.10 billion in free cash flow, up 81% year-over-year, a 34.1% non-GAAP operating margin, and continued optimism around Anthropic, Benioff has little reason to panic.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

For now, at least.

Per-share earnings rose from $5.24 on January 31, 2023, to an estimated $16.75 for the fiscal year ending January 31, 2027, according to stock market research tool TIKR.

That said, TIKR projects a clear dip the following year, to $16.02. This suggests analysts expect Anthropic, and likely OpenAI, to start eating into Salesforce's already-declining share of the global CRM market. In November 2022, IDC Research showed Salesforce leading the CRM market with a 22.9% share. In 2025, its share was 20%, according to IDC. That's a decline of about 3 percentage points in three years, before Anthropic or OpenAI went public or saw widespread adoption. Both companies are pushing further into enterprise and making it an essential part of their businesses, so they could take more of Salesforce's CRM market share.

Another concern is that Salesforce is buying back a large amount of its own stock. In March, the company announced a $25 billion accelerated share repurchase. In other words, banks delivered most of the shares upfront rather than Salesforce buying them gradually on the open market. The buyback was funded by a $25 billion debt issuance, a minor red flag. Its diluted share count fell from 962 million to 821 million in a year, a decline of about 15%. That means a meaningful part of its per-share growth comes from fewer shares and more debt, not just from the business itself.

We're not saying this means it's over, but it's hardly a sign of strength. It's something to watch as Anthropic, and likely OpenAI in 2027, turns CRM, SaaS, and the rest of tech on its head.

title: How much Salesforce stock does CEO Marc Benioff actually own?
detail:
How much Salesforce stock does CEO Marc Benioff actually own?
Laura Rodini, Jeremy Salvucci
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 11:13 AM CST 4 min read
CRM
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff founded his company in 1999, he looked to another corporate giant for inspiration.

Benioff was "intrigued" by Amazon's business model and how it changed the way consumers shopped, he wrote in his memoir, Behind the Cloud. He figured he could harness the emerging power of the Internet to revolutionize the business world, too.

Fast-forward more than 25 years, and Salesforce has done just that. By offering business applications as a service over the internet (SaaS), it transformed the way companies operated.

Salesforce was valued at $1.1 billion at its 2004 IPO; in 2026, it's worth around $179.2 billion — an increase of more than 10,000%.

Benioff has been handsomely rewarded for his company's success. And while he remains CRM's largest individual shareholder, he has also made philanthropy a cornerstone of the company's mission.

Here's a closer look at his ownership in the company and how he acquired so many shares.

How much of Salesforce does Marc Benioff own? 

According to Salesforce's 2026 Proxy Statement, Benioff owns 22,791,882 shares of Salesforce, equating to about 2.8% of the company.

Based on Salesforce's closing share price of $217.84 on Monday, November 16, Benioff's stake is worth approximately $4.89 billion.

Related: How much SBUX stock does Starbucks' former CEO Howard Schultz own?

Is Benioff the largest individual shareholder of Salesforce?

Yes. The company's other biggest individual shareholders include Mason Morfit, a Salesforce board member and co-CEO of ValueAct Capital, who owns approximately 2,994,509 shares through his investment firm, according to Salesforce's 2026 Proxy Statement.

Interestingly, not all of Salesforce's founders have publicly disclosed shareholdings.

In 1999, Benioff teamed up with Parker Harris, Dave Moellenhoff, and Frank Dominguez and incorporated the business. 

Harris remains on Salesforce's Board of Directors and currently serves as the CTO of Slack, which Salesforce acquired in 2021. He owns approximately 2,332,259 shares of CRM.

Software architect Dave Moellenhoff left the company in the early 2000s, and his holdings are not publicly disclosed.

Frank Dominguez helped develop the foundation for Salesforce's pioneering cloud-delivery (SaaS) system, but he also left the company in 2009. Any remaining share ownership he has is not publicly disclosed.

Related: How much MSFT stock does former CEO Steve Ballmer actually own?

How & when did Benioff accumulate his CRM stock?

Over his nearly three-decade tenure as the head of Salesforce, Benioff regularly accumulated shares through his ownership as a founder and through equity-based compensation awards. According to Forbes, he owned approximately 40 million shares in the company as of July 2014, representing about 6.5% of its outstanding shares at the time.

Salesforce (CRM) slid about 9% as software stocks weakened ahead of Anthropic's massive IPO, which put renewed attention on whether AI agents could eventually reduce the need for traditional paid seats.

The heavy one day drop fits into a wider losing stretch for Salesforce, with the 30 day share price return down about 11% and the year to date move lower by roughly 15%. However, the 90 day share price return is still up around 10%, which suggests earlier momentum has faded as investors reassess AI agent risks, recent security headlines, and the implications of Anthropic's IPO. As a result, the 1 year and 3 year total shareholder returns, down about 9% and 3% respectively, remain in negative territory.

Seize this pullback in Salesforce as a chance to reassess your tech exposure and scan for other software players showing resilient momentum with the 35 high quality undervalued stocks.

After a 9% single-day slide and a year-to-date decline of about 15%, Salesforce is no longer priced as if everything has gone right. The key question is whether more of the potential upside now lies ahead for investors or if it is already in the rear-view mirror as the valuation resets.

Most Popular Narrative: 16% Undervalued

On the Simply Wall St Community fair value, Salesforce screens as undervalued, with a narrative estimate of $255.90 against a last close of $214.83 and a 9% discount rate shaping that view.

According to michaelyang, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the narrative, the current debate around AI agents and seat-based pricing is missing the real asset inside Salesforce.

The per-seat licence was only ever the toll booth. The asset is the governed system of record: every customer, every deal, every entitlement, for about 80% of the Fortune 500. And the one thing an autonomous AI agent cannot do is act on a customer without getting into that record first. An agent with no permissions, no governance and no audit trail is not an asset, it is a liability waiting to happen. So the same automation wave that threatens the seat count is exactly what drives every serious enterprise deeper into the data layer Salesforce owns. The meter changes from per-person to per-action. It does not disappear.
